title: 道德經 第四十九章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 49, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 77. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 49 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 任德 (Trusting to Potency). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
聖人無常心，
以百姓心為心。

morph.gloss: the sage — the one who acts as this book describes
to have not, to be without
the heart-mind — thinking and feeling in one organ, never merely emotion
with, by means of — the first half of the frame 以 A 為 B, 'take A as B'
the hundred clans — the common people, named by their family lines
a hundred; by extension, the whole lot of them
wéi: makes, takes as — the second half of 以 A 為 B
heart-mind — his own, the possessor left unsaid

sentences.l:
The sage: no abiding heart-mind;
he takes the hundred clans' heart-mind as his heart-mind.
sentences.i: The sage has no fixed mind of his own; he makes the mind of the people his mind.
sentences.n:
以 A 為 B is the standing classical frame for 'take A as B, let A serve as B'. 為 is wéi: it has a nominal complement, but there is nothing benefactive or causal about it, so the house default holds.

心 is the heart-mind — thinking and feeling in one organ. English has to choose a word and neither 'heart' nor 'mind' is right on its own. What the line claims is that the sage keeps no settled view, preference or purpose of his own for the people to run up against.

常心 stays two taps, exactly as 常道 does in chapter 1: nobody has christened it, and it means just what its parts mean. The Mawangdui manuscripts put the words the other way about — 聖人恆無心, 'the sage constantly has no heart-mind' — which makes the emptiness permanent rather than making the heart unfixed. (恆 héng is those manuscripts' word throughout where the received text has 常; the received text changed it to avoid the personal name of the Han emperor Liu Heng.)

sentences.t:
善者，吾善之；
不善者，吾亦善之，

morph.gloss: the one who — turns what precedes it into a noun
the SAME character as a verb governing an object: to be good to, to do well by
him, them — the object pronoun, not the genitive
as a verb again: to be good to

sentences.l:
One who is good — I am good to him;
one who is not good — I am also good to him,
sentences.i: Whoever is good, I do well by; whoever is not good, I do well by too —
sentences.n:
善 does three different jobs inside these two short lines, and nothing whatever marks the shifts: it is the adjective 'good'; 者 then makes a noun of it, 'the one who is good'; and 吾善之 has the same character as a transitive verb, 'I am good to him'. This fluidity of part of speech is the central fact of Classical Chinese grammar. Position is the only signal, and there is nothing to look up.

之 here is the object pronoun 'him', not the genitive 'of'. The character does both jobs constantly and only its neighbours tell you which one is running.

The speaker changes without warning. The unit before spoke of 聖人 in the third person; this one says 吾, 'I'. Classical Chinese has no quotation marks, so whether the sage has begun to speak or the author has stepped forward is left open.

morph.gloss: potency — the power a thing has by being what it is; but see the note

sentences.n:
Two characters with nothing between them, and the parsing is genuinely argued over.

Read as written, 德 is this book's own great word — the potency a thing has by being what it is, the 德 of its title — and 善 is predicated of it with no verb 'to be', as usual: 'potency: goodness'. That is the graph the edition prints, and it is what this text follows.

The other reading takes 德 as a loan graph for its homophone 得 dé, 'to get, to obtain', which early texts write for it freely: 'and so goodness is got'. Many editors take this, and it is not a weak reading. The difference is real: on one account goodness is what the sage has, on the other it is what his conduct produces in the people. Wang Bi's own comment on the passage turns on goodness not being lost, which is compatible with either, so the crib does not settle it and we say so.

sentences.t:
信者，吾信之；
不信者，吾亦信之，
德信。
聖人在天下歙歙，
為天下渾其心，

morph.gloss: trustworthy, as good as one's word
the same character as a verb: to trust
potency — the same crux as 德善 above
the sage — the one who acts as this book describes
to be in, to stand in the midst of
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world, and everyone in it
drawn in and drawn in — a doubled descriptive of bearing: pulled shut, giving nothing out (歙 is the opposite of 張 'to spread open')
to draw in, to contract, to suck shut
wèi: for the sake of — a benefactive complement, so not the default wéi
all under heaven — the whole inhabited world, and everyone in it
to muddy, to churn until nothing in it can be told apart
his — whose, the line does not say; see the note

sentences.i: Whoever is true to his word I trust; whoever is not, I trust as well — potency, then, is trust. In all under heaven the sage holds himself pulled in; for the sake of all under heaven he lets his own mind run muddy,
sentences.n:
信 repeats exactly the manoeuvre 善 made two units ago — adjective, then noun with 者, then transitive verb — so the couplet is built to be read against that one. 德信 is the same crux as 德善.

歙 is 'to draw in, to suck shut'. Doubled, 歙歙 describes a bearing rather than an act, like 昭昭 and 悶悶 in chapter 20: the sage stands in all under heaven pulled shut, putting nothing out. The doubled word is not secure, either: other recensions of the received text print a different reduplicated word here whose sense is 'anxious, apprehensive', which would make the sage wary of the world instead of self-effacing before it. Wang Bi's text has 歙歙, and his comment takes it as the sage keeping nothing fixed in his heart, which is the reading given here.

為 is wèi here. 為天下 is 'for the sake of all under heaven', a nominal complement in plainly benefactive sense, which is the one case where the house default gives way. 渾 is water stirred until nothing in it can be distinguished.

Whose heart-mind is muddied? 其心 does not say — Chinese pronouns often have no stated antecedent, and this one has none. We read it as the sage's own: Wang Bi's comment runs that way, glossing the line as the sage having nothing he sets his heart on, and the chapter has just said he keeps no heart-mind of his own. Read the other way it is the people's hearts that he blurs together into one, which would make him a manager of others rather than a man who has given up having a mind of his own.

sentences.t:
百姓皆注其耳目，
聖人皆孩之。

morph.gloss: the hundred clans — the common people, named by their family lines
a hundred; by extension, the whole lot of them
all of them — an adverb, standing before the verb and not before the noun
to pour into, to fix upon — of eyes and ears, to be trained on something
the sage — the one who acts as this book describes
all of them — here counting the OBJECT, not the subject: the sage is one man, and it is 之 'them' that 皆 gathers up
a babe in arms — here as a VERB: to make an infant of, to babe them

sentences.l:
The hundred clans all pour their ears and eyes;
the sage makes babes of them all.
sentences.i: The people all strain their ears and eyes toward him; the sage turns them all back into children.
sentences.n:
孩 is the noun 'a babe in arms' used as a verb — 'he babes them'. It is the strongest instance of the chapter's one grammatical lesson, because English has no verb at all to put opposite it; 'makes children of them' is as close as it comes.

皆 is an adverb and stands before the verb, so in the first line it counts the hundred clans, who are many. In the second the subject is one man, and what it gathers up is the object: he babes them all.

其耳目: the ears and eyes are the people's own, and the line does not say what they are trained on — 注 'pour' is left without a goal. The idiomatic supplies 'toward him', the sage being the only other party in the sentence; the literal leaves the gap open. The Mawangdui manuscripts read 屬 zhǔ, 'to fasten on, to fix upon', where the received text has 注 'to pour into' — the same picture drawn with a different brush.

Whether the closing line is tender or chilling the text does not settle. The newborn is this book's standing figure for what is whole and unspoilt; it is also a figure for someone who cannot think for himself, and a reader in the fourth century BC, when this was advice to rulers, would have heard both.
